html:
A financial collapse in Lebanon that came into the open in 2019. Banks froze savers' deposits and the Lebanese pound lost almost all its value. The World Bank has ranked it among the worst economic crises anywhere since the mid-1800s.

For two decades the central bank, under its long-serving governor Riad Salameh, had held the pound at a fixed rate to the dollar. To do so it needed a constant inflow of dollars. Banks drew in deposits, much of them from the diaspora, with high interest and lent them on to the central bank and the state, which spent heavily and ran up huge debts. Critics later compared the scheme to a pyramid that worked only as long as new money came in.

When the inflow dried up, the system broke. In October 2019 mass protests broke out against the political class. Banks closed for two weeks and then let people take out only small sums. In March 2020 the state defaulted on its foreign debt. The pandemic and the Beirut port explosion of August 2020 made everything worse.

Savings built over lifetimes vanished. Many fell into poverty, and doctors, nurses and young graduates left the country in large numbers.
